chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Aban ibn Uthman from Shu'ayb al-Aqarqufi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
He was asked, while I was listening nearby, about the divorce of a slave. He said: He does not have the authority to divorce, nor to marry.
Do you not hear God, the Exalted, saying: 'A slave owned, who has no power over anything'?
He said: He has no power to divorce, nor to marry, except with the permission of his master.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This report and the first report, although they are general in that he does not possess the right of divorce, we have specified them because when he is married to his master's female slave, since we have explained in the preceding chapter that if he is married to another master's female slave or to a free woman, then his divorce is valid, and the second report from this chapter indicates that. Therefore, for this reason, we specified them as we mentioned.
ai.seo_question: Does a male slave have the right to divorce his wife in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration from Abu Abdillah al-Sadiq (AS), who derives the slave's lack of independent marital authority directly from the Quranic attribute of 'powerlessness' (la yaqdiru 'ala shay'). Muhammad ibn al-Hasan provides crucial jurisprudential specification (takhsis), clarifying that this restriction applies specifically when the slave is married to his own master's slave, whereas his divorce remains valid if married to a free woman or another master's slave, resolving apparent generality in the text.
